title: Neurobehavioural consequences of repetitive prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on pathological aggression (Subproject B01 of the TRR379)
summary:
Aggressive and violent behaviors are major challenges for both offenders and victims and is a significant burden on the socioeconomic system. Therapeutic approaches to improve behavioral control and reduce aggression show only moderate success. The neural mechanisms of provocation-related violence in violent offenders and patients with mental disorders remain largely unexplored and studies on the effectiveness of methods to reduce and prevent this behavior are rare. 

Aggression is associated with deficits in the frontal regions of the brain that are related to the inhibition of behavior. These frontal brain regions serve as regulatory mechanisms that can inhibit impulsive behaviors. Previous studies suggest that violent offenders have deficits in frontal brain regions, which can lead to emotional dysregulation and aggression.  The complexity and diversity of aggression make treatment challenging and underscore the need for personalized approaches such as non-invasive brain stimulation techniques. This has proven to be a promising approach among the various treatment methods to improve the inhibition of aggression. This project aims to investigate the effects of non-invasive brain stimulation techniques on aggression and cognitive control processes measured.

This project aims to investigate the effects of repetitive tDCS on aggression and cognitive control. During the 4-day study the participants will undergo several questionnaires and behavioural tasks both in and outside the MRI Scanner. Day 1 (approx. 4 hours) includes questionnaires, interviews, cognitive tests, and three behavioural tasks conducted in the MRI Scanner. On day 2 (approx. 30 minutes), stimulation is applied during a behavioral task in the MRI. On day 3 (approx. 2 hours), three behavioural tasks are conducted again in the MRI. On day 4 (approx. 30 minutes), during a follow up session the lasting effects of tDCS are examined during a behavioural control task without stimulation, outside the MRI. The procedure for the violent offender on day two requires more time as two additional interviews for the cohort will be conducted. We collect data on behavioural patterns including aggression and behavioural control. These behaviours are analysed through specific tasks, while imaging techniques are used to further investigate brain functioning. In addition, the project aims to identify individual difference to predict responsiveness to tDCS.
conditions: Violent offenders, patients with mental disorders, and drug use problems

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Gender: Male
Minimum Age: 18
Maximum Age 40

Right-handedness

Offenders: Conviction for at least one violent crime
Patients with mental disorder: Substance use
Exclusion criteria:
Acute or chronic neurological disorders
MRI contraindications
tDCS contraindications
Healthy controls: Acute or chronic psychiatric disorders and conviction for violent crimes
